title: Long-lost characters reappear through a tendency transmitted each generation

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Long-lost characters reappear through a tendency transmitted each generation

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: When a character lost in a breed reappears after many generations, the cause is a tendency to produce that character transmitted in every generation which at last prevails under favourable conditions, not a sudden resemblance to a distant ancestor.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: When a character which has been lost in a breed, reappears after a great number of generations, the most probable hypothesis is, not that the offspring suddenly takes after an ancestor some hundred generations distant, but that in each successive generation there has been a tendency to reproduce the character in question, which at last, under unknown favourable conditions, gains an ascendancy.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter V, “Laws of Variation”; section “Reversions to long-lost characters.”. Scope: domestic breeds and wild species

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch05-15: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.49

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern genetics can test Darwin's transmission model in documented recent cases. Existing data rarely span enough generations to distinguish all proposed routes for long-lost characters.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For pedigreed reappearance events, test whether causal ancestral alleles or regulatory states were transmitted cryptically through intervening generations and became expressed under particular genetic or environmental conditions. Demonstrated continuous transmission supports the claim; a genuinely new mutation producing the resemblance refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Historical breed pedigrees and DNA over hundreds of generations are unavailable.

Reappearance can arise from retained alleles, epigenetics, recombination or new mutation.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.57
data existence: 0.54
data adequacy: 0.35
analysis feasibility: 0.5
discriminating power: 0.49

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Allele age can separate latent transmission from a sudden reconstitution, which is the empirical contrast in the wording, but only where genomes and pedigrees coincide. Those cases are few and mostly domestic, far from a general law for breeds and wild species. The mapping from a tendency in every generation onto standing variation is reasonable and still interpretive, so the present data support case studies rather than a general resolution.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For traits that reappear after many generations of absence, test whether the alleles are old segregating variants or recurrent new mutations. Old standing variation would support a tendency transmitted through the intervening generations; de novo mutation recreating the phenotype would support sudden reappearance. Only a few domestic breeds have both the phenotype records and the genomes.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The transmitted tendency is not directly observed and is inferred from allele age.

Well-genotyped atavisms are a handful of domestic cases.

A phenotype can reappear by either standing variation or new mutation in the same breed.

fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.4
data existence: 0.42
